scenario_prompt: Write a short demo script for a live discovery session, showing the specific capability the buyer asked to see rather than a generic product tour. Context: the buyer's VP of Infrastructure said in discovery he wants 'a perimeter we can actually govern,' referring to replacing manual failover across a 620-virtual-machine on-premises estate. The demo should show a governed project perimeter being applied to a representative workload on the target cloud platform. Return only the demo script text.
text:
I don't have discovery notes or transcript beyond the quoted line — treating "a perimeter we can actually govern" and "620 virtual machines" and "manual failover" as the only customer-supplied terms; nothing else is customer source material, so everything else is judged by the deletion test alone. Proceeding with the draft now.

**Artifact family: demo or discovery material**

---

**Opening reframe**

Today, failover across your 620-VM on-premises estate is a manual process — someone has to notice, decide, and act before a workload comes back up. You told us you want a perimeter you can actually govern. This demo shows one project boundary, applied to one representative workload, doing that governance and that failover without a person in the loop.

**Scene 1 — Before: the ungoverned state**

We start with a workload that mirrors a typical VM in your estate: [PF-2.4 GAP: which representative VM class or workload profile from your estate this demo instance mirrors — not yet named]. Right now, moving or recovering it depends on a person following a runbook. There is no single boundary that says what this workload is allowed to do, where it can run, or who can touch it.

**Scene 2 — Applying the governed perimeter**

We define a project-level perimeter around this one workload: identity, network, and policy rules attached to the project, not to the VM. On screen, you'll see the perimeter's rules — who can deploy into it, what regions it can fail into, what it can never reach. [PF-1.17 GAP: a named, checkable comparable — a prior deployment, benchmark, or reference architecture — showing this perimeter model applied at comparable scale has not been supplied]

**Scene 3 — After: governed failover, demonstrated live**

You will watch the platform detect a simulated zone failure and move the workload to its designated failover target inside the same perimeter — no manual step, no separate approval outside the policy already defined. [PF-2.14 REVIEW (commitment): confirm before this ships that "no manual step" is accurate for the demo's actual failover path, not just the happy-path scenario shown live] Compare that to today: a person notices, a person decides, a person acts, once per VM.

**Scene 4 — Tie it back to your estate**

This is one workload out of 620. [PF-1.13 GAP: your current mean-time-to-recover or failover-completion figure for the on-prem estate has not been stated — without it we cannot show the before/after time comparison quantified] The perimeter model you just saw is what would be replicated across the estate, project by project, so the boundary — not a person — is what governs failover.

**Close, addressed to the VP of Infrastructure**

You said you want a perimeter you can actually govern. What you just saw was that perimeter enforcing itself — the rule set, not a runbook, deciding what happens when something fails.
